Dyno Ellipse

CurvesAlgebraGeometry
Game: Two spinning arms pull a pen along a curve; watch the shape they make together.
How to play: Slide the four controls to change each arm's length and turning speed. Press Go to start or stop, tick the boxes to show the circles and arms, and press Reset to start again.
Look for the math

Richard Mickelsen wrote to Alexander Bogomolny with a surprise: add two circular motions turning at the same speed in opposite directions, and the tip of the sum draws an ellipse. The old applet let you change the speeds and lengths of both motions. This page keeps its four controls and its drawing exactly.

Two arrows, one pen

Start both arrows pointing right. At step n the first tip is at (r1 cos(n·Rate1/360), −r1 sin(n·Rate1/360)) and the second at (r2 cos(n·Rate2/360), −r2 sin(n·Rate2/360)). These are vectors in screen coordinates, with y growing downward. The pen sits at their componentwise sum, which is the same as a parametric curve. The divisor is 360 radians, not degrees: a full turn at speed 1 needs 720π steps. Both arrows have zero phase in the applet; the page explains that shifting time and turning the axes can always make the phases zero, so nothing is lost.

Why the sum is an ellipse

Set Rate2 = −Rate1. Because cosine is even and sine is odd, the two x parts add and the two y parts subtract: X = (r1+r2) cos(wt) and Y = −(r1−r2) sin(wt). Square and add:

(X/(r1+r2))² + (Y/(r1−r2))² = 1

The curve has semi-axes r1+r2 and |r1−r2|. The logic test checked this identity at every speed from 1 to 50, every pair of lengths from 0 to 100, and many steps; the largest error was below 2×10−12. The page's formula has a plus sign on Y because it measures y upward; squaring makes the two statements the same.

The two easy extremes

When the speeds are equal the two arrows never separate, so the pen runs round a circle of radius r1+r2. When the speeds are opposite and the lengths are equal, the y parts cancel exactly and the pen runs back and forth along a straight line segment of length 2(r1+r2). Both are verified over the whole range of speeds and lengths.

Other speeds, other curves

The page also names curves for other ratios W = Rate1/Rate2 and R = r1/r2: W=2, R=1/2 gives a cardioid, W=−2, R=1/2 a deltoid with three cusps, W=−3, R=1/3 an astroid with four, and W=3, R=1/3 a nephroid with two. The test measured the cusps of each curve from its own tangent and found 1, 3, 4 and 2 respectively, as claimed. For any whole W, R = 1/|W| gives an epicycloid with W−1 cusps or a hypocycloid with W+1.

Set Turn 1 to 2, Turn 2 to −2 and both lengths to 60: the pen draws a straight line. Change Length 2 to 40 and watch the line open into an ellipse. The old applet also had an unused “number of rays” control left over from another program; it changed nothing, so this page leaves it out.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
